title: Reduced motion is part of the craft
metaTitle: Prefers reduced motion, treated as craft
excerpt: Prefers reduced motion means you ship two versions: the move you intended, and a still or instant version when someone asks the system for less motion.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. The still room fits a piece about pages that stay calm when motion is reduced.
caption: The still version is a design, not a broken animation. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is prefers-reduced-motion?
faqs.answer: It is a system setting, exposed to the page as a CSS media feature, that says this person wants less motion. Your site reads that preference and swaps to a calmer version of each move. It is not a browser quirk. It is a request you can honor or ignore.

faqs.question: Does reduced motion mean no animation at all?
faqs.answer: It means you remove or shorten motion that is decorative, large, or vestibular. An instant state change, or a simple fade of opacity, is often enough. The meaning of the interface has to remain. If a step only makes sense while something flies across the screen, the step was under-designed.

faqs.question: Who is this for?
faqs.answer: For people who get sick or distracted when interfaces move, and for anyone who turned the setting on because they prefer a calmer screen. You will not know which visitor is which, so the setting is the signal. WCAG's purpose is a shared standard so more people can use web content, and honoring the setting is part of that standard of care.

markdown:
Prefers reduced motion is a request the visitor has already made in their system settings. The craft is to ship two versions of a move. The intended one, for people who have not asked for less. A still or instant version, for people who have. Both versions should look designed. The reduced one is not the animated page with the keyframes ripped out until the layout collapses.

Hanabi treats that pair as part of done on a marketing site. A transition can be beautiful and still be optional. If the only way to understand the page is to watch something travel, the page is unfinished for anyone who will never watch it.

## What the setting is asking for

Operating systems let a person say they want less motion. Browsers expose that as the media feature `prefers-reduced-motion`. A stylesheet can ask whether the preference is reduce, and serve different CSS. Nothing about the person's medical history is sent to you. The bit is the whole message: fewer and smaller movements, please.

Honor the bit. Do not wait for someone to find a toggle buried in your footer, although a site-level control can be a welcome extra. The system setting is the one they already took the trouble to turn on. Ignoring it means your intro sequence plays for the exact person who asked the computer not to do that.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes the guidelines as a shared standard for making web content more accessible to people with disabilities. Content includes text, images, and the code that presents them. The principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Motion sits across the first three. A change that is only visible as movement may not be perceivable to everyone. A control that dances may be harder to operate. A step that is understandable only if you saw the animation is not understandable on the still page.

This article does not certify anyone's site. WCAG conformance is a specific claim against success criteria, and a blog post cannot make it for you. The practical bar is smaller and still serious: if the system says reduce, your signature animation does not play.

## Two versions, designed on purpose

List every move on the page. For each one, write the reduced version beside it before you implement either.

A hero that fades and rises becomes a hero that is simply there. A menu that slides in from the side becomes a menu that appears in place, or fades opacity without traveling. A carousel that auto-advances stops advancing. A button state changes color or label instantly instead of bouncing. A page transition cuts, or cross-fades so briefly that it does not feel like travel.

Opacity and color can still change. Position changes across large distances are the ones to remove first. Autoplaying video and looping backgrounds stop. Nothing should parallax. The reading order and the layout stay the same in both versions, so you are not maintaining two websites. You are maintaining two behaviors on one layout.

Put the meaning in the thing that both versions share. The dialog has a title. The error has a sentence. The new panel is in a sensible place in the document. Motion, when it runs, agrees with that structure. It does not replace it. Then the reduced version is automatically coherent, because you did not hide the plot inside the move.

## How to build it without a second product

In CSS, wrap the travel in a query. The default can be the fuller motion if that is your intended craft, and the reduce branch sets the duration to nearly nothing, or removes the transform. The safer emotional default for a long-lived tool is the reverse: modest motion always, and still less when asked. Marketing pages sometimes want the richer move. They still need the branch.

Do not only gate the CSS. JavaScript that calls a timeline, a library such as Motion, or a scroll scene has to check the same preference. Otherwise the stylesheet is quiet and the script is not. One helper that returns whether to animate, used by every transition, beats a scavenger hunt six months later when a new effect ships without the check.

Test it the way a person sets it. On macOS, in the accessibility display settings. On iOS, in the motion settings. On Windows, in the visual effects settings. Turn it on, reload, and walk the page. Open the menu, submit the form, follow the anchor. You are looking for anything that still travels, loops, or plays on its own. Then turn the setting off and confirm the intended version still exists. Teams sometimes fix the bug by deleting all motion, which fails the half of the design that was legitimate.

## What reduced motion is not

It is not a reason to ship a careless still page and call the animated one the real site. The still page is what some of your visitors will only ever see. It needs hierarchy, contrast, and an obvious action. If it looks like a wireframe, you used motion as decoration for an unfinished layout.

It is not an announcement in the footer that says we care about accessibility, while the hero video autoplays. The setting is the test. The sentence is optional.

It is not only for a small group you can decide does not include your customers. You do not know who has the setting on. Some of them are buyers. Some of them are you, on a day when a busy page is hard to look at. The cost of the second version is low when you plan it with the first. The cost is high when you retrofit a page that was storyboarded as a single film.

## A review before launch

Turn the preference on. Read the homepage. Use the primary action. Open and close every overlay. Scroll the length of the page.

- Does anything move on its own?
- Does any object travel a long distance?
- Is every state still clear without the travel?
- Can you finish the main task?

If the answer to the last question is yes, and the first two are no, the craft held. If you find a move that has no still equivalent, write the equivalent before you discuss whether the animation is delightful. Delight is allowed. A single version of delight is not.

Accessibility is the wider bar this sits inside. [Accessibility as a design quality bar](/blog/accessibility-as-a-quality-bar) is the next piece, on contrast, focus, names, and reduced motion as part of done rather than as a late audit.

When you want that pair of versions built into the site, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Reduced motion is part of the work, not a setting to discover after launch.
